archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-stuffing, pass-leaking)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff with a defense that stops the run and tackles well but cannot cover, and an offense that controls the clock without the quarterback play or line health to finish drives.

report.headline: Ball-control offense, league-worst pass defense, and a quarterback room in pieces
report.take:
Mike LaFleur's first Cardinals team at 3-7 looks a lot like the 2022, 2023 and 2025 Arizona teams that lost 13 or more games. The losing comes from a defense that can't stop the pass, and it carries over from year to year: the defense ranked 31st in EPA allowed in 2023 and 26th last season, and it is 28th now. A new coach hasn't changed the core problem. The points allowed are 31st in the league, and the 184-289 scoring line is what you'd expect from that.

The defense is really two units. Against the run it is good: 8th in rush EPA allowed, 3rd in missed-tackle rate, 6th in EPA allowed to lead backs. Against the pass it is the worst in the league at 0.276 EPA per dropback, 29th on deep throws and 28th in explosive pass rate. With a pass rush 25th in pressure rate, quarterbacks get time to throw over the top. It has only 7 takeaways (29th) and allows touchdowns on 70% of red-zone trips (27th), so it rarely gets the stop or the turnover that would hide the coverage. On offense, the success rate (12th), time of possession (4th) and short-yardage conversions (3rd) say the Cardinals can grind out drives. A passing game 24th in EPA, behind a line 27th in pressure rate allowed, keeps those drives from turning into touchdowns.

Two things in the numbers deserve care. Yards allowed per game sits 17th, which looks ordinary. The damage is in where the yards come: chunk passes and red-zone touchdowns, not long drives. The record is also about what the team has earned. The point differential implies 2.6 wins against 3 actual. Those wins came against a Chargers offense now ranked 32nd, in an 18-16 upset at the Rams as 12.5-point underdogs, and in a 33-30 shootout at a Dallas defense ranked 32nd. The quarterback split also needs a qualifier. Brissett's offense put up 30 at San Francisco and 33 at Dallas. Minshew's two starts produced 3 and 6 points, but they came against Seattle and the Rams, defenses ranked 5th and 3rd, so not all of that collapse belongs to him.

Where it goes from here depends on who plays. Minshew is out for the season with a torn UCL. The center (100% of snaps), a guard and a tackle are all out. The secondary has lost safety Andrew Wingard for an extended stretch, which hurts a pass defense that was already the league's worst. The dossier doesn't say who starts at quarterback in Kansas City. Brissett started the first eight games and isn't on the injury report. After the Chiefs, the schedule turns soft: five straight opponents with losing records and defenses ranked 22nd or worse, then San Francisco. This team can still win a few more games, mostly in shootouts where it outlasts bad defenses, but nothing here points to a team turning a corner.

strengths.title: Run defense that tackles
strengths.body: Arizona is 8th in rush EPA allowed and 3rd in missed-tackle rate, and lead backs have done little against it. Sound fits and tackling account for this, not just game script, and the history doesn't suggest it's a fluke. Losing linebacker Jordan Burch and DT Zachary Carter thins the front, so expect it to slip a little rather than collapse.

strengths.title: Possession and short-yardage offense
strengths.body: The offense holds the ball (4th in time of possession), converts short yardage at the 3rd-best rate and keeps a respectable success rate. That is a coherent plan for a team that needs to keep its pass defense off the field. It depends on the line, and three linemen are now out, including the every-snap center.

strengths.title: McBride and Wilson as anchors
strengths.body: Trey McBride (99 targets) and Michael Wilson (88) take most of the targets, which gives any quarterback simple, reliable reads. That matters with a quarterback change forced on the team. A tight end who draws that volume holds up whoever throws to him.

concerns.title: The league's worst pass defense
concerns.body: Opponents gain more per dropback against Arizona than against anyone else, and deep throws hurt it most. A weak pass rush gives coverage little help, and the safety group just lost Wingard for an extended period. Given that the defense ranked near the bottom in 2023 and 2025 too, this is a structural flaw, not a bad stretch.

concerns.title: Quarterback and line falling apart
concerns.body: The two Minshew starts produced 3 and 6 points, ending with a -13.8 passing EPA game against the Rams before his season-ending elbow injury. The line already ranked 27th in pressure rate allowed with everyone healthy, and now the center, a guard and a tackle are out. Tough defenses explain part of the drop, but the personnel behind center and up front is weaker than it was in October.

concerns.title: No stops where it matters
concerns.body: Seven takeaways and a 70% red-zone touchdown rate allowed mean opponents finish drives against this defense. This isn't bad turnover luck. A defense that doesn't pressure the quarterback doesn't force mistakes, so expect it to continue.

trend.note: The Brissett stretch was uneven but competitive, with three wins including a shootout at Dallas in Week 8. Then the offense collapsed in the two Minshew starts, scoring 3 and 6 points against top defenses, and the quarterback and line injuries since then make a quick rebound unlikely.

nextGame.headline: A banged-up Arizona heads to Kansas City as a 16.5-point underdog
nextGame.body:
This is the worst possible matchup for Arizona's defense. Kansas City's offense ranks 4th in EPA and throws well above expectation (2nd in pass rate over expected), and it now faces the league's worst pass defense. The Chiefs also lead the league in yards per carry, so the one part of Arizona's defense that works, its run defense, gets tested too. Going the other way, Kansas City's defense is 3rd in points allowed, 5th in rush EPA allowed and 2nd in red-zone touchdown rate allowed, which hurts an offense that depends on grinding drives. The one opening is that the Chiefs rarely pressure the quarterback (29th in pressure rate), and they funnel an unusually large share of targets to tight ends. The Book's KC -16.5 and Arizona's +1000 moneyline reflect all of this.

Availability tilts it further. Arizona is without its center Hjalte Froholdt, guard Jon Gaines and tackle Jayden Williams. Safety Andrew Wingard is out for an extended period, linebacker Jordan Burch is done for the year and DT Zachary Carter is on IR. Minshew is out for the season, and the dossier doesn't name the starter. Brissett, who started the first eight games, isn't on the report. Kansas City is missing lead back Kenneth Walker III, tackle Jaylon Moore and DT Peter Woods, with guard Trey Smith questionable after a concussion. That weakens the Chiefs' run game and their line somewhat, but Patrick Mahomes has started every game.

waysToWin.title: Shorten the game with possession
waysToWin.body: Arizona ranks 4th in time of possession and Kansas City 25th, and a 41.5 total already projects few possessions. If Arizona converts short yardage and keeps Mahomes on the sideline, a big spread becomes a one- or two-score game late. The catch is that the Chiefs' run defense ranks 5th in EPA allowed, so the drives will have to come through short passes as much as through runs.

waysToWin.title: Feed McBride against a TE funnel
waysToWin.body: Kansas City sees an above-league share of targets go to tight ends, and lead tight ends have scored above their usual output against it. Kansas City also allows almost nothing to opposing WR1s, which takes Wilson out of the picture. That makes McBride the natural place to go, especially for a quarterback working behind a patched line. Quick throws to the tight end limit how much the depleted line has to hold up.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden yards
waysToWin.body: Kansas City's special teams rank 31st in EPA per game, so field position is one area where Arizona can find an edge. A short field or a special-teams mistake is the most realistic way for this offense to get points against a defense this stingy in the red zone. Arizona's own special teams are below average, so this is an opportunity, not a strength it can count on.

waysToLose.title: Mahomes picks apart the secondary
waysToLose.body: A pass-heavy Kansas City offense against the league's worst pass defense, now without Wingard, is the most likely way this gets out of hand. Arizona's poor pressure rate means Mahomes should have time to throw deep, where Arizona ranks 29th. If the Chiefs hit two or three explosive passes early, Arizona is forced into the passing game it can't run well.

waysToLose.title: Patched line, stalled drives
waysToLose.body: Without its center, a guard and a tackle, a line that already allowed pressure at the 27th-ranked rate now faces a defense that is 3rd in points allowed. The last time this offense saw a top run defense it ran for 34 yards against the Rams. If early downs fail, the ball-control plan is gone by halftime.

waysToLose.title: Red-zone trips end in field goals
waysToLose.body: Kansas City allows touchdowns on only 36.8% of red-zone trips, 2nd in the league, while Arizona's defense gives up touchdowns on 70% of its own. Even a good day moving the ball loses badly if Arizona trades field goals for touchdowns.

nextGame.watch: Who starts at quarterback, and whether the interior line can hold up without Froholdt for the first few series. If early drives stall, a 16.5-point spread starts looking small.

restOfSeason.body:
The pass defense is the constant, and it will keep costing Arizona games. It has been bottom-tier across several seasons, generates little pressure, and has just lost a starting safety. The run defense and the possession offense are real, but both depend on bodies the injury report is taking away, including the starting center. What softens the outlook is the schedule. After Kansas City come Washington, Philadelphia, the Jets, New Orleans and Las Vegas, all with losing records and all with defenses ranked 22nd or worse. Then San Francisco closes the season.

Expect Arizona to give up points to almost everyone and to win only the games it can turn into shootouts against bad defenses, the way it beat Dallas. The quarterback situation determines how many of those it wins. If Brissett returns and plays like he did in October, the offense should reach the high teens or low 20s against these defenses. If not, the three- and six-point outings are more likely than a fluke. Picking up one or two more wins is the realistic middle outcome.
swingFactors: Who starts at QB after Minshew's injury
Return of the center and guard to the line
Whether the soft middle of the schedule turns into wins

confidence.note: Ten games paint a consistent defensive picture, but the QB situation and line injuries cloud the offense.
